description: §1.2, Example 1.4, Step 4 (boundary state i=m): the derived value contradicts the model as stated in the same example. The problem statement says "an arrival that finds the counter full is turned away", and Step 4 repeats "an arrival is turned away and cannot change the state". Under that rule the blocked arrival is lost, so the count at the end of the slot is m - D, giving p_{m,m-1} = q and p_{mm} = 1 - q. The note instead boxes p_{m,m-1} = q(1-p), p_{mm} = 1 - q(1-p), and then justifies it as "a departure and no (accepted) arrival" — but the factor (1-p) can only appear if an arrival IS accepted when a departure frees a slot in the same slot, i.e. exactly the opposite of "turned away". The wrong value propagates: Example 1.5 quotes p_{10,9}=0.32, p_{10,10}=0.68 (should be 0.40 / 0.60 under the stated rule), computes/g5_s1.py key B_pmm=0.68, the §1 cheatsheet bullet "p_{m,m-1}=q(1-p), p_{mm}=1-q(1-p)", the Fig. 1.4 caption and alt-text, and the widget line `P[m][m-1] = q*(1-p); P[m][m] = 1 - q*(1-p)`. Fix: either state the admission rule as "an arrival is accepted if a departure frees a slot in the same slot" (keeping q(1-p)), or keep "turned away" and change the boundary row to p_{m,m-1}=q, p_{mm}=1-q, rerunning the compute and the widget.

§1.2, Example 1.4, Step 3: the stated reason why p_{01}=p rather than p(1-q) is wrong. The text says "the interior formula charges the arriving customer with the possibility of being served away in the same slot". In the Step-2 derivation D_{n+1} is defined as the departure of "the customer in service", i.e. a pre-existing customer — the arriving customer is never served in its own slot in any interior state either. The correct reason is that at state 0 nobody is in service, so D_{n+1} ≡ 0 and the (1-q) factor simply is not there. As written it also directly contradicts Practice 1.9, which concludes the model already forbids same-slot service of an arrival.

§1.2, Gotcha "the within-slot convention is part of the model" vs. Practice 1.9: mutually contradictory. The Gotcha asserts that "an arriving customer cannot be served in the slot in which it arrives, or an arrival is only accepted after the departure is processed" is "a different but equally defensible convention" that "changes p_ii and the boundary rows". Practice 1.9 then works that very convention out and correctly concludes nothing changes ("the interior row is again p_{i,i+1}=p(1-q), p_{i,i-1}=q(1-p), p_{ii}=pq+(1-p)(1-q)") because it is the convention already adopted. One of the two must be rewritten: the genuinely alternative convention is the opposite one — an arriving customer CAN be served in its own slot (giving p_{01}=p(1-q)) — which is what Practice 1.9's last sentences describe.

§1.4, Interpretation box, item 1: "by n=10 they agree with the limit in six decimals" is numerically false. computes/g5_s1.json A_r_n10 = 0.2857185035 vs π₁ = 0.2857142857; the gap is 4.22e-6 (computes/g5_s0.json two_state_convergence_gap["10"] = 4.2178e-06), so the values agree to five decimals, not six. The same paragraph then says "about log(10⁻⁶)/log(0.3) ≈ 11.5 steps buy six decimals", which contradicts the claim. Fix to "five decimals by n=10" (or "by n≈12 for six"). Note the identical phrasing in Practice 1.1 ("by n=10 both rows have become (0.75,0.25) to six decimals") IS correct there, since λ=0.2 gives an error of 2.6e-8.

§1.2, Practice 1.4, final sentence: "with no self-transitions the fortune has the same parity as n until absorption" is backwards for this chain. X_n ≡ X_0 + n (mod 2), and X_0 = 1, so X_n has the parity of n+1 (after 1 round the fortune is 0 or 2, both even, while n=1 is odd). Say "X_n has the parity of X_0 + n", which is what actually forces r_{11}(2)=0.

§1.2, Example 1.5, "Long run" paragraph: "Reverse the parameters to p=0.5, q=0.3" is inaccurate — reversing p=0.2, q=0.4 would give p=0.4, q=0.2. The numbers 0.5/0.3 are a new pair (they match computes keys B2_p_up=0.35, B2_p_down=0.15, so the arithmetic is right). Reword to "Now take p=0.5, q=0.3, so that arrivals outrun service".

§1.3, Theorem (Chapman–Kolmogorov): stated "For all n>1". The recursion is equally valid at n=1 (r_{ij}(1)=Σ_k r_{ik}(0)p_{kj}=Σ_k δ_{ik}p_{kj}=p_{ij}), and the note itself supplies r_{ij}(0)=δ_{ij} two paragraphs earlier. State it for n≥1 with initial condition R(0)=I, which is also what the matrix form R(n)=R(n-1)P, R(0)=I, in the very next box assumes.

§0.3, Question C, last sentence: "by the geometric mean of G2 §3 it lingers 1/0.6 = 1.666667 steps". "Geometric mean" is a different, unrelated quantity; the intended reference is the mean of a geometric random variable. Reword to "by the mean 1/p of a geometric random variable (G2 §3)".

Fig. 0.1, right panel (notes/img/g5_s0_memory.png): the two-state diagram is drawn with the 1→2 and 2→1 arcs crossing into a lens/bowtie whose arrowheads sit immediately beside the source nodes, so the arc directions are not readable — and the alt-text describes something else ("an upper arc from 1 to 2 and a lower arc from 2 back to 1"). §2.3, Recipe item 4 (positive-matrix test): "For the two classes of Fig. 2.2 the smallest such n is 2 for both" does not match the criterion as stated immediately before it ("there exists n≥1 and a state i from which all states of the class are reachable in exactly n steps"). For class {3,4,5}, state 3 reaches 3, 4 and 5 in exactly one step (p_33, p_34, p_35 all > 0), so the smallest such n is 1; likewise state 6 reaches 6 and 7 in one step. The value 2 in the compute keys warmup_class1_first_all_pos_n / warmup_class2_first_all_pos_n is the smallest n for the all-pairs condition (r_ij(n)>0 for every i,j in the class). Attach the sentence explicitly to the all-pairs form.

§2.1, derivation of "transient states are visited finitely often": the final step equates two differently-conditioned quantities. N is defined as the number of visits to i given the chain is currently at i (that is what justifies P(N≥k) ≤ ρ^{k-1}), but the conclusion uses E[N] = Σ_{n≥0} P(X_n=i), which is the expected number of visits from an arbitrary/unconditional start. Add the missing line: from any start the number of visits is at most 1 + N (0 if i is never reached), so the expected visit count is finite from every start, and hence Σ_n P(X_n=i) < ∞ and P(X_n=i) → 0.

A Poisson with integer mean mu is doubly maximized at mu-1 and mu — here p_K(5) = p_K(6) = 0.160623 exactly (5^... check: 6^5/5! = 6^6/6! = 64.8).
